aipc01-0003.takeaway: Use hierarchical chunking when retrieval needs small matching units but generation needs their broader parent context.
options: Child chunks support precise matching; replacing them with their parent chunks supplies surrounding context for the answer.
Small fixed chunks can match precisely, but this configuration has no parent expansion to recover the surrounding section.
Treating a whole manual as one chunk loses the small retrieval units the scenario requires.
Overlap repeats adjacent text; it does not create a child-to-parent retrieval relationship.

aipc01-0005.takeaway: For cross-language semantic retrieval, choose an embedding model designed to represent the required languages in a shared vector space.
options: Titan Multimodal Embeddings targets image-and-text similarity; that capability does not establish support for this multilingual text-search requirement.
Cohere Embed Multilingual supports cross-lingual search with one multilingual text-embedding model, matching the requested architecture.
Separate language indexes add routing and maintenance work and contradict the requirement to keep one embedding architecture. They do not by themselves solve cross-language matching.
BM25 matches lexical terms. It does not produce semantic embeddings that connect equivalent meanings across languages.

aipc01-0007.takeaway: Enforce retrieval scope before returning chunks: derive department filters from authenticated permissions in trusted application code.
options: A department attribute and a server-enforced query filter restrict the shared index to the caller's authorized documents. Do not let callers choose an unrestricted department value.
Separate knowledge bases can isolate departments, but require the additional indexes and operations the scenario wants to avoid.
Post-filtering allows unauthorized chunks to reach the application first and can leave too few relevant results after filtering.
A content-safety guardrail does not replace document authorization or reliably establish which department a caller may access.

aipc01-0011.takeaway: Use supervised fine-tuning to learn task behavior, tone, and formatting from labeled examples when prompting has proved insufficient; evaluate the result before release.
options: The labeled examples teach the desired input-to-output behavior and style by updating model parameters, matching the stated need.
RAG supplies examples as inference-time context but does not train the model to follow their style consistently.
Continued pre-training targets adaptation from raw domain text, rather than directly learning the labeled input-to-output behavior available here.
More examples increase each request's context and cost; the scenario already says prompt instructions have not met the consistency requirement.

aipc01-0013.takeaway: Choose customer managed KMS keys for customer control and key-use auditing, and configure each storage layer, including the vector store and S3, as applicable.
options: Default AWS owned encryption protects stored data, but does not give the bank control of the encryption key's policy or lifecycle.
Customer managed KMS keys provide policy and lifecycle control and auditable KMS activity. Apply them to the relevant Bedrock resources and backing stores; one setting does not cover every layer.
A hardcoded key exposes key material and lacks the managed access controls and audit trail requested for these service resources.
Security groups restrict network traffic; they neither encrypt stored artifacts nor provide customer control over encryption keys.

aipc01-0021.takeaway: For a large tool catalog, retrieve relevant tool definitions before asking the model to choose an operation.
options: Gateway semantic tool selection searches by task context so the agent can surface relevant tools without sending every schema in each prompt.
Sending the entire catalog preserves the prompt-size and tool-choice problems identified in the scenario.
One general-purpose tool still needs to express and validate many distinct operations; merging names alone does not discover the relevant capability.
Random selection can omit the required operation, leaving the agent unable to complete otherwise supported requests.

aipc01-0022.takeaway: Use Converse to share message handling across supported Bedrock models; still check feature support and any model-specific parameters.
options: Converse provides a common message request and response structure, reducing model-family adapters when testing supported models.
An adapter per model family can work, but requires maintaining the separate serialization and parsing code the team wants to reduce.
Batch inference processes asynchronous collections of requests; it does not provide the interactive chat interface needed here.
Moving to separately hosted SageMaker endpoints adds deployment work, and a common runtime transport does not make every model's payload identical.

aipc01-0023.takeaway: Place stable prompt content before changing content and cache the reusable prefix on a supported model; verify cache hits and net savings.
options: Retrieving the style guide changes context assembly and adds retrieval work; it does not directly reuse the model's repeated prefix processing.
The output ceiling does not reduce the repeated instruction tokens that dominate input processing.
A checkpoint after the static prefix makes it eligible for reuse across questions, reducing input processing on cache hits subject to model limits and cache lifetime.
Changing API serialization does not remove or cache the repeated 8,000-token prefix.

aipc01-0024.takeaway: For transient throttling, bound retries and spread them with exponential backoff and jitter; retries cannot create sustained capacity.
options: A tight retry loop adds traffic while the service is already rejecting excess load, making recovery harder.
Failing immediately gives recoverable throttling no opportunity to clear, reducing successful completion during short bursts.
A fixed delay can synchronize concurrent Lambda instances so they send the next burst together.
Increasing delays reduce retry pressure, randomized jitter separates callers, and an attempt limit bounds waiting and retry work.

aipc01-0026.takeaway: Semantic vector search needs embeddings, with documents and queries encoded in a compatible embedding space.
options: A summarization prompt returns generated text; that text is not a dense vector ready for nearest-neighbor comparison.
Grounding checks assess whether an answer is supported by supplied material; they do not build article vectors for an index.
A text-embedding model converts article text into numerical vectors intended for semantic similarity search.
Tool use lets the model request application functions; it does not itself encode text into search vectors.

aipc01-0027.takeaway: Streaming must work through every hop. Lambda function URLs support RESPONSE_STREAM; API Gateway REST proxy integrations can also stream when explicitly configured.
options: A streaming-enabled function URL and a Lambda handler that forwards chunks give the browser an incremental response through the listed direct path.
A larger timeout permits a longer request but does not change buffering. API Gateway REST needs STREAM transfer mode and a compatible streaming integration.
Collecting all chunks before returning recreates the buffering that delays the user's first visible token.
Batch inference produces asynchronous completed results; polling it does not deliver an interactive token stream.

aipc01-0028.takeaway: Use a state machine when the requirement is explicit sequencing, branching, retries, and failure visibility across multiple services.
options: A large Lambda can implement the workflow, but the team must write and maintain its branching, retry, and execution-tracking logic.
EventBridge routes events, but rules alone do not supply this whole branching workflow with a single execution history.
SQS decouples stages and buffers work; queues alone do not define the conditional sequence or track the complete execution.
Step Functions expresses tasks, choices, retries, and failure paths in a state machine with managed execution visibility.

aipc01-0038.takeaway: Use ApplyGuardrail to evaluate content independently of where the generating model runs, and enforce its result before forwarding input or releasing output.
options: Custom regex and keywords would duplicate only part of the managed policy and create separate implementations to maintain.
InvokeModel calls a model available through Bedrock; it does not turn an arbitrary external endpoint into a Bedrock invocation.
ApplyGuardrail accepts content for evaluation against the existing guardrail independently of model inference, so both applications can reuse the policy.
WAF protects web traffic using web-security rules; it does not execute the existing Bedrock semantic content-safety policy.

aipc01-0039.takeaway: Match the policy to the problem: denied topics for subjects, word filters for phrases, and sensitive-information filters for identifiers. Test coverage across phrasings.
options: Word filters match configured words or phrases; an enumeration cannot reliably describe the whole concept of personalized advice.
A denied topic defines the prohibited subject semantically using a description and examples, making it the best policy fit without guaranteeing perfect detection.
Lower temperature changes sampling randomness, not whether personalized advice is an allowed topic.
A PII policy detects personal identifiers and patterns; a request for financial advice need not contain any such identifier.

aipc01-0042.takeaway: Combine detection of malicious input with enforced limits on tool actions. A missed prompt attack must still face authorization checks.
options: The prompt-attack filter adds detection of malicious user instructions. Configure the input scope or tags required by the invocation API and test the filter.
Least-privilege tools, IAM, and Gateway policy constrain authorized actions outside the model, limiting damage when detection misses an attack.
A system instruction can help guide behavior, but it is not an authorization boundary that prevents a tool from executing.
Larger models can still follow injected instructions; model size does not provide immunity or replace enforced permissions.
Higher temperature adds output variation without restricting what tools the agent may invoke.

aipc01-0044.takeaway: Use Macie for managed sensitive-data discovery in S3, then remediate findings separately before training; discovery alone does not sanitize the corpus.
options: Guardrails evaluates submitted inference content; it is not a managed discovery job over a multi-terabyte S3 training corpus.
Macie inventories S3 data and runs sensitive-data discovery with findings, matching the bulk classification and reporting requirement.
CloudTrail records object API activity, such as reads and writes, rather than classifying the sensitive content inside files.
Comprehend can detect PII in supported text, but manually processing individual objects adds extraction, scheduling, and reporting work at this scale.

aipc01-0045.takeaway: Use a cross-account role with a trust policy and scoped permissions to obtain temporary credentials for centrally governed resources.
options: A policy attached directly to a base foundation model is not the cross-account access mechanism offered for that model resource.
IAM user access keys create the long-lived credentials the design specifically needs to avoid.
Public invocation removes the identity and authorization controls required for centrally governed model and guardrail access.
STS AssumeRole provides temporary credentials in account B. The trust policy, caller permission to assume the role, and the role's scoped Bedrock permissions establish the access path.

aipc01-0053.takeaway: For interactive latency, evaluate latency-optimized inference on a supported model and Region; measure actual tail latency because quotas can cause standard-mode fallback.
options: Batch inference waits for asynchronous processing and is unsuited to an immediate voice reply.
A larger output limit allows longer answers; it does not make each generated token arrive faster.
A queue can smooth load, but waiting for capacity adds to the user's response time.
Latency-optimized inference directly targets response time for supported models. Check the served configuration and measured latency rather than treating the option as an SLA guarantee.

aipc01-0059.takeaway: Use an automated judge with a defined rubric for repeated semantic-quality scoring, and calibrate its judgments against expert review.
options: Human review can supply valuable judgments, but reviewing thousands of summaries every release does not meet the request for automatic scoring.
Reference-based similarity metrics alone do not establish factual faithfulness or capture every aspect of coherence and conciseness.
An LLM judge can score the team's dataset against the specified dimensions and produce explanations at release scale. Its scores still need validation against the intended quality standard.
Summary length is an operational measurement, not evidence that the summary is coherent or supported by its source.

aipc01-0060.takeaway: Separate retrieval relevance from answer groundedness: on-topic passages can still produce an answer containing unsupported claims.
options: High context relevance does not support irrelevant retrieval as the primary diagnosis. Replacing embeddings would not directly address unsupported generated claims.
Low groundedness means the answer is insufficiently supported by the supplied passages, even when those passages and the answer are on-topic.
Acceptable answer relevance gives no evidence that ambiguity is the main issue; relevance and evidential support are separate dimensions.
More documents do not directly fix unsupported generation when the reported retrieved context is already relevant. Inspect the answer against its actual passages first.

aipc01-0062.takeaway: Classify the exception before fixing it: throttling calls for rate control and capacity investigation, while authorization and validation failures require different changes.
options: Bounded backoff with jitter handles bursts; for sustained demand, investigate the applicable quotas and supported capacity options before choosing an increase or Provisioned Throughput.
Missing invocation permission produces an authorization failure; peak-only ThrottlingException is evidence of a different problem.
Changing the output ceiling is not the general fix for ThrottlingException. Token-based quotas can matter, so inspect the actual rate and token limits rather than assuming a context-window error.
Invocation logging supplies diagnostic evidence; enabling it does not resubmit failed requests.

aipc01-0064.takeaway: After offline checks, use a limited production rollout with quality and business measures, explicit promotion criteria, and a rollback path.
options: Immediate replacement exposes every user, and an error-rate alarm can miss fluent but lower-quality answers.
A small treatment group and a current-version control reveal production effects while limiting exposure before expansion.
A larger offline dataset can improve confidence but cannot measure actual production business effects or limit the later all-user cutover.
Provisioned capacity addresses serving throughput; it neither compares prompt quality nor restricts which users receive the new prompt.

aipc01-0118.takeaway: For bulk work that can wait, consider batch inference on a supported model, checking job quotas, pricing, and completion time against the deadline.
options: Repeatedly reserving peak real-time capacity adds capacity-management work and can leave paid capacity idle between nightly runs.
Aggressive retries increase pressure on the same on-demand limits instead of moving the workload to an appropriate asynchronous path.
Latency optimization targets interactive response time; it does not address the overnight bulk-processing cost objective.
Batch inference reads prepared inputs from S3 and writes results asynchronously to S3, matching a large workload whose results can wait.

aipc01-0120.takeaway: For native team-level on-demand cost allocation, invoke through tagged application inference profiles and activate the relevant billing cost-allocation tags.
options: Budget alerts report thresholds against available cost dimensions; adding alerts does not create a missing team attribution dimension.
Separate accounts can provide attribution, but require an organizational change and reconciliation that application profiles can avoid for this requirement.
A profile per team provides a tagged invocation resource for cost attribution when teams actually use their assigned profile ARNs.
Invocation logs support usage analysis and may identify callers, but manually guessing teams from logs is weaker than the requested tagged billing breakdown.

aipc01-0124.takeaway: When Retrieve omits the answer passage, inspect retrieval filters and indexed chunks before changing the answer-generating model.
options: The generator's context limit applies after retrieval; it does not explain a passage already absent from a direct Retrieve result.
A mismatched metadata predicate can remove the correct document from eligible results before it reaches generation.
A missing permission produces an access failure; it is not a mechanism that silently replaces the relevant passages with unrelated ones.
Throttling reports a failure rather than substituting unrelated retrieved content as a successful response.
Splitting related facts across chunks can weaken the evidence and semantic match available in any one result, making chunk inspection and retrieval testing appropriate.

aipc01-0128.takeaway: Version prompts and evaluation data together, then enforce a quality threshold in CI; a stable procedure improves comparisons without making model scores deterministic.
options: A few manual checks can miss representative failure cases and do not provide the requested automated merge gate.
Waiting for production complaints discovers regressions after users are exposed and does not prevent merging them.
Prompt management stores and versions prompts; it does not itself run the team's quality evaluation or enforce a CI threshold.
A versioned evaluation set and a failing CI check turn the agreed quality threshold into a pre-merge safeguard. Calibrate thresholds for judge and generation variability.

aipc01-0410.takeaway: Prompt caching reuses prefix processing on a cache hit. It changes input processing cost and time, while the model still generates a new response.
options: A successful cache read uses the model's cached-input price, reducing the cost of those reused input tokens.
Reusing prefix processing can reduce time-to-first-token; actual improvement depends on the workload and model.
Cached tokens still belong to the prompt context; caching does not enlarge the model's context window.
Prefix reuse reduces input processing, not the sequential work of generating each output token, so proportional output-speed gains do not follow.
Caching does not reserve serving capacity or guarantee throughput; dedicated capacity is a separate serving choice.

aipc01-0498.takeaway: Distillation can start with representative prompts: the teacher generates responses used to train the smaller student, with quality validated on held-out examples.
options: Human-labeled prompt-response pairs can help, but are not mandatory when the teacher can generate responses from supplied prompts.
Bedrock can generate teacher responses for the team's prompts and use that synthetic data to fine-tune the student.
CloudTrail management events audit API activity; they are not the exclusive source of prompt-response training data.
Prompt caching reuses inference prefixes and is not a prerequisite or replacement for preparing a representative distillation dataset.

aipc01-0621.takeaway: Start model selection with the required output modality, then verify the chosen model's lifecycle and Regional availability.
options: Stable Image Ultra is a text-to-image generator, and its model card lists US West (Oregon), matching the required output and Region.
Nova Micro produces text; it does not generate the product-image pixels requested here.
Titan Text Embeddings V2 encodes text into vectors for similarity tasks rather than creating new images.
Cohere Embed English encodes text for retrieval or similarity; an embedding is not a generated product image.

aipc01-0650.takeaway: Use Titan's embedded watermark and surviving Content Credentials as provenance evidence, with explicit limits after edits or metadata removal.
options: Bedrock watermark detection checks for the invisible signal embedded in generated images; modified images can be harder to detect reliably.
C2PA Content Credentials carry signed generation provenance when the metadata is retained and verifiable.
An application-captured SHA-256 hash can establish an exact file match, but it is not a provenance signal Titan automatically attaches.
An application-added logo is a separate visible mark, not Titan's built-in invisible watermark or Content Credentials.
Ordinary application-added EXIF tags are separate editable metadata and are not the signed Content Credentials specified here.

aipc01-0680.takeaway: Exchange the enterprise assertion for a role session before signing AWS service calls.
options: A SAML assertion authenticates the federation exchange. It is not the credential used to sign ordinary Bedrock API requests.
This uses the SAML federation API and includes the session token required with temporary AWS credentials.
ExternalId is a condition value for AssumeRole, not a SAML assertion exchange. Omitting the session token also breaks temporary credential use.
A console sign-in token creates console access; it is not the AWS credential set used to sign CLI service requests.

aipc01-0681.takeaway: Application JWTs and AWS request-signing credentials serve different authorization paths.
options: A longer JWT lifetime does not convert the token into AWS request-signing credentials.
An identity pool provides the documented bridge from user pool identity tokens to temporary AWS credentials.
Role claims can inform role selection, but a claim containing a role does not itself supply temporary AWS signing credentials.
The authenticated role defines AWS permissions; the returned credential set supplies the AWS signing material.
User pool OAuth scopes authorize application token use; they do not turn an access token into the AWS access key, secret and session token required here.

aipc01-0682.takeaway: Diagnose OIDC trust claims separately from the permissions of the resulting role session.
options: This aligns the actual subject with the intended production trust boundary without expanding who can deploy.
The Bedrock action matters after role assumption; it cannot satisfy the mismatched OIDC subject condition.
This expands trust to other repositories and branches, violating the main-only production requirement.
AssumeRole uses AWS credentials; AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the appropriate exchange for the OIDC token.

aipc01-0683.takeaway: Cross-account AssumeRole needs both source permission and target trust.
options: The source principal needs permission to call AssumeRole for the target role.
That grants the opposite assumption direction; it does not authorize the engineer in A to assume the target in B.
The target trust relationship must admit the source principal or allow the source account to delegate access.
PassRole permits passing a role to a service; it does not authorize assuming a cross-account role session.
GetSessionToken is not the cross-account exchange and cannot replace the two required policy relationships.

aipc01-0684.takeaway: Preserve the session token whenever temporary AWS credentials cross an application boundary.
options: The request already has an authorized role; changing a resource policy does not supply its missing session token.
The AWS session token must be the value issued with the temporary credentials, not the SAML assertion used to obtain them.
This preserves the complete credential set required to authenticate the assumed role session.
The credentials are still valid. A longer lifetime cannot repair a request missing its session token.

aipc01-0685.takeaway: Credential refresh means acquiring a new session through a valid provider, not extending an expired key.
options: Changing a local timestamp cannot change the server-side expiration of an STS credential set.
Backoff helps transient service failures, but it cannot make an expired credential valid or extend its lifetime.
A supported provider lets the client resolve and renew credentials rather than retaining a static expired snapshot.
An application access token cannot renew an STS credential set. The provider must obtain a new valid AWS session.
The provider must still be able to authenticate its refresh exchange; an expired upstream login can require renewal.

aipc01-0686.takeaway: Use session policies to reduce a role session's permissions, not to expand them.
options: Session policies do not replace the role with an independent permission grant; they cannot exceed its identity permissions.
Trust policy conditions govern assumption, while service permissions belong in authorization policies.
These policies intersect rather than union. The denial is expected and is not evidence of service unavailability.
Only A is allowed by both policies, so the observed A/B behavior matches the configured session boundary.

aipc01-0687.takeaway: Check both role duration and SAML assertion expiration when sizing a federated API session.
options: The role already permits the requested duration; the assertion still limits the session to 10:00.
A renewed authorized exchange can obtain replacement credentials rather than relying on the expiring session.
The API explicitly honors the shorter assertion lifetime, so the original credentials do not last until 13:00.
Console session settings do not extend the existing API credential set issued by STS.

aipc01-0688.takeaway: A target role's maximum duration does not override the one-hour role-chaining limit.
options: Changing the source role duration does not remove the target chained session's one-hour limit.
A session policy controls permissions, not the STS role-chaining duration limit.
This keeps the chained request within the documented limit and provides a path for continued authorized work.
AssumeRole expects the target IAM role ARN; a session ARN does not bypass the duration rule.

aipc01-0689.takeaway: Match identity pool role trust to both the intended pool and the intended authentication state.
options: This admits signed-in identities through the correct role while preserving the identity pool restriction.
This expands guest access and leaves the authenticated role trust mismatch unresolved.
For the identity pool principal, aud identifies the identity pool, not the user pool app client.
The aud restriction is required for identity pool role trust; an email domain is not a substitute pool identifier.

aipc01-0690.takeaway: Provision the delivery connection as well as the logging source and destination.
options: CloudTrail audits API activity; its trail configuration is not the connection between a vended log source and destination.
Model invocation logs describe a different logging path and do not complete this ingestion delivery configuration.
CreateDelivery explicitly connects the existing source and destination; active delivery is the relevant configuration check.
StartIngestionJob accepts a client token and description, not a logGroupName that creates logging delivery.

aipc01-0691.takeaway: Source permission and destination policy setup are separate parts of ingestion log provisioning.
options: This is the documented source-side permission for allowing knowledge base log delivery.
Reading source documents is different from authorizing vended logs to the destination bucket; broad source access does not fix these gaps.
Invoking a model is unrelated to granting permission to configure delivery for the knowledge base resource.
Direct writes to a CloudWatch log group do not configure the required S3 destination bucket permissions for vended delivery.
The documented S3 delivery setup uses these permissions on the destination bucket to establish its resource policy.

aipc01-0692.takeaway: Validate final document status and chunk outcomes; a single successful retrieval cannot establish complete ingestion.
options: A successful query covers surviving chunks; treating failures only as a quality warning does not establish complete document ingestion.
Changing chunking may be an experiment after diagnosis, but retry acceptance does not establish that the failed chunks were successfully indexed.
The final PARTIALLY_INDEXED status and failed chunk creations are document coverage evidence, not merely a batch-throughput measurement.
This respects the final document outcome and uses the logged failures to drive targeted recovery.

aipc01-0693.takeaway: Use stage-specific failure records and their reasons to select the next diagnostic step.
options: This follows both the failed stage and the explicit write-authorization reason in the scenario.
Read access for the query client does not fix the write rejection reported for the knowledge base ingestion path.
Changing the application caller session does not repair vector-store access for the role already bound to the knowledge base ingestion job.
Capacity tuning is appropriate for throughput pressure, but the supplied failure reason identifies an authorization rejection that unchanged permissions will preserve.

aipc01-0694.takeaway: Trace ignored-resource reasons and validate metadata sidecar naming before changing retrieval behavior.
options: The problem is ingestion of metadata; returning more chunks does not correct an ignored metadata resource.
This uses the relevant diagnostic record and the documented sidecar naming convention.
There is a direct metadata configuration clue; changing the generation model does not repair that input.
CloudTrail captures API activity and attribution, not a replacement stream of file-level ingestion decisions.

aipc01-0695.takeaway: Gate on ingestion outcomes tied to the run, not on acceptance of the start request.
options: 202 accepts asynchronous work; it does not prove indexing completion.
The API returns the job status, failure reasons and document counters needed for run-level verification.
Job-correlated resource records identify document and chunk failures for the specific release being evaluated.
A model can generate fluent text without demonstrating that the new documents were indexed.
HTTP 200 means the status lookup succeeded, not that the returned ingestion job succeeded.

aipc01-0696.takeaway: Cross-account log delivery needs destination-account authorization in addition to the source configuration.
options: Source-side permission alone does not create the destination-account authorization that the scenario says is missing.
Changing ingestion service trust can break knowledge base operation and does not configure destination delivery authorization.
This installs the documented cross-account permission at the correct logical delivery destination.
Model invocation logging is a different configuration and does not grant the missing cross-account delivery permission.

aipc01-0697.takeaway: Use the resource status field and a run identifier together when selecting ingestion failures.
options: Both predicates target the required run and the specific resource failure stage.
ingestion_job_status is the job-level status field; DELETION_FAILED belongs to the resource event.status field.
OR admits all J-new records and deletion failures from old runs, producing the mixed evidence the incident must exclude.
This selects a different failure stage and misses the deletion failures under investigation.

aipc01-0698.takeaway: Model job states and document states separately, and inspect outcome details at the appropriate level.
options: A successful lookup can return a failed or active job; the status field remains necessary.
COMPLETE is a documented ingestion-job terminal state, not a lookup failure.
Initial acceptance is represented by the start response; COMPLETE does not mean the monitor should await a document-only state.
This fixes the enum mismatch while retaining meaningful job and document outcome checks.

aipc01-0699.takeaway: Combine API attribution with ingestion execution logs when an incident spans both initiation and processing.
options: CloudTrail is the documented source for who made an API request, when and from which request context.
Ingestion log examples identify the resource and job; they are not a substitute for CloudTrail API caller attribution.
The audit event records the API action, while downstream asynchronous ingestion can still fail.
File status, status_reasons and chunk_statistics are the relevant ingestion diagnostics.
Management API auditing does not replace resource-level processing transitions emitted by APPLICATION_LOGS.

aipc01-0700.takeaway: Keep S3 source state consistent with direct knowledge base changes so later syncs preserve the intended lifecycle.
options: A retrieval threshold does not remove obsolete source content or prevent re-ingestion.
A prompt instruction does not repair the source-index mismatch or reliably establish document removal.
Direct deletion does not create a permanent exclusion for an object that remains in the S3 source.
This removes the source that can reintroduce the content and distinguishes requested deletion from verified completion.

aipc01-0701.takeaway: Persist an idempotency token before sending; reuse it for uncertain retries of that operation.
options: This uses the documented idempotency mechanism without treating the network outcome as ingestion completion.
A new token identifies new work and defeats deduplication of the uncertain original submission.
A later intentional refresh is new work; reusing a previous token can suppress it.
Transmission is not acceptance or completion, and omitting the saved token loses the available idempotency protection.

aipc01-0702.takeaway: Use a stable custom document identifier for updates and verify the replacement outcome.
options: Random IDs create distinct documents and leave obsolete copies unless the application separately removes them.
The submitted dataSourceType must match the connected source, and S3 source content is not supplied inline this way.
The stable identifier updates the intended document instead of adding another identity for the same procedure.
Custom sources use document operations without a sync; StartIngestionJob does not accept a document ID as described.

aipc01-0703.takeaway: Batch within a verified contract and track each document through its actual processing outcome.
options: Idempotency tokens do not bypass request-size or schema rules, and one batch violates the stated application contract.
202 acknowledges asynchronous ingestion; pending or active document states are not final success.
This respects the eight-document contract and preserves identities for later outcome tracking.
GetKnowledgeBaseDocuments supports these bounded lookups and exposes the document states needed by the contract.
A shared custom identifier causes overwrites instead of representing 24 independent documents.

aipc01-0704.takeaway: Deletion has a request phase and a verified outcome; preserve document identity across both.
options: 202 accepts asynchronous work, and the returned DELETE_IN_PROGRESS explicitly says processing is active.
This preserves the mapping between the retention request and the documents still being removed.
A new identifier creates another document identity; it does not remove the eight originals.
TopK truncates query results and cannot establish that a document is absent from the index.
Document-state and reconciliation evidence let the workflow distinguish processing, failures and confirmed removal.

aipc01-0705.takeaway: Use durable per-key sequencer checks to stop stale events from undoing newer index state.
options: Arrival order is not guaranteed to match operation order, which is the exact failure demonstrated.
Sequencers are comparable for the same key, not a global ordering across different objects.
The incoming PUT precedes the applied delete, so skipping it preserves the later intended state.
Unequal-length raw string comparison is unsafe; left-padding produces 00ff, which sorts before 0100.

aipc01-0706.takeaway: Buffer bursts, bound consumer concurrency, and make retries safe; concurrency limits alone do not provide exactly-once processing.
options: This implements the stated two-consumer budget without creating a lower reserved-concurrency bottleneck.
The settings conflict with both the two-invocation budget and the documented requirement to provision enough function concurrency.
Standard queues can deliver duplicates, and a larger batch alone does not make downstream mutations safe.
Early deletion can lose updates when the downstream request fails; an empty queue would hide dropped work.
Idempotent processing protects against redelivery while retry handling preserves work during transient ingestion failures.

aipc01-0707.takeaway: Design refresh scheduling for deletes as well as creates and updates.
options: Incremental sync explicitly handles removed documents, so a full vector-store rebuild is unnecessary.
This closes the missing deletion path while preserving the existing incremental refresh architecture.
Invocation logging records a different activity and does not create the missing source-removal trigger.
A generation prompt does not propagate storage changes into the knowledge base index.

aipc01-0708.takeaway: Authorize document lifecycle APIs explicitly and scope them to the knowledge bases the worker manages.
options: Model invocation is separate from the document lifecycle actions and does not resolve this denied operation.
PassRole is not the permission to ingest or delete knowledge base documents, and all-role scope is unnecessary.
Full service access exceeds the stated one-knowledge-base lifecycle requirement.
These actions match the worker's write and inspection responsibilities at the intended resource scope.

aipc01-0709.takeaway: Coordinate ingestion writers and preserve the source of truth before reconciliation runs.
options: Distinct tokens identify distinct requests; they do not prevent simultaneous direct-ingestion and sync submissions or keep S3 consistent.
This conservative coordination rule prevents execution overlap, rather than merely sequencing HTTP submissions while asynchronous processing continues.
Per-key event ordering can reject stale updates, but it does not satisfy the separate rule against overlapping these ingestion methods.
This prevents a later sync from reconciling against stale S3 content that contradicts intended direct changes.
Outcome monitoring is useful, but a successful direct change still needs consistent S3 source state before later syncs reconcile it.

aipc01-0710.takeaway: An asynchronous serving engine and a SageMaker asynchronous endpoint are separate configuration decisions.
options: Disabling async mode and changing dynamic batch delay does not select the async integration.
These settings select the documented LMI v15 async integration while retaining real-time endpoint invocation.
This combines the historical lmi-dist rolling-batch path with the different v15 async path rather than selecting the required entrypoint.

aipc01-0857.takeaway: When invoking a managed prompt version, respect which configuration belongs to the prompt resource.
options: This field is also prohibited with a managed prompt ARN and cannot provide an override bypass.
Converse disallows these overrides when modelId is a prompt ARN; the versioned resource supplies them.
Direct invocation can work but no longer executes the claimed reviewable prompt resource.
Creating another draft does not change the request-field restrictions for the versioned prompt invocation.

aipc01-0858.takeaway: Return-control results must be correlated with the action that the agent actually requested.
options: This preserves the action-group identity required by the return-control protocol.
A renamed deployment identifier is not the action-group identity returned for the pending invocation.
Business idempotency identifiers may also be useful but cannot replace the agent protocol correlation identifier.
Transport request correlation does not replace the outstanding agent invocation identifier.
This associates the result with the outstanding invocation.

aipc01-0859.takeaway: Handle return-control continuation and a new user instruction as distinct protocol events.
options: This can process the new request but abandons the outstanding continuation and useful conversation context.
When return-control results are supplied, inputText is ignored; a separate request preserves the new user turn.
This repeats completed work and loses correlation rather than sequencing the new user request.
Attributes provide turn context but do not establish that the ignored inputText has been processed as a separate user request.

aipc01-0860.takeaway: A successful backend call still needs the action-group Lambda response contract.
options: Serialization alone does not supply the required action-group envelope and operation metadata.
The API-schema action group expects this envelope and serialization rather than an API Gateway proxy response.
The configured action group uses an API schema, which requires its corresponding response structure.
The domain payload still needs the action-group wrapper and explicit operation identification.

aipc01-0861.takeaway: Use the function action-group response state that lets the agent seek missing information.
options: This converts an unresolved ambiguity into an apparently successful operation on the wrong possible location.
REPROMPT returns information to the model for another attempt rather than treating the dependency as failed.
The agent can interpret empty inventory as a real business result instead of asking for the missing location.
The missing city will remain missing; retries of the same ambiguous input do not solicit clarification.

aipc01-0862.takeaway: Choose attributes according to their session or turn lifetime, and verify identity outside model context.
options: Prompt-session attributes intentionally apply to one invocation turn.
Model-generated prose is not a reliable persistent store for verified application context.
Session attributes are the supported mechanism for context across turns in an unexpired session.
This prevents the new request from receiving the intended session continuity.
Session attributes persist; they do not provide the locale's required one-turn lifetime.

aipc01-0863.takeaway: Tool execution results should retain their structured correlation with the assistant tool request.
options: The result must identify the tool request it satisfies; a fresh ID does not do so.
The model conversation also needs the corresponding assistant tool-use message.
This retains conversation text but still omits the structured result-to-request correlation.
The assistant message plus the matching toolResult supplies the protocol link needed for the next model response.

aipc01-0864.takeaway: Prompt substitution and invocation metadata have different roles; preserve prompt-version evidence.
options: The prompt configuration under test differs even if the model is identical.
promptVariables is the request map for values used by the managed prompt.
Additional messages do not populate the named template variable.
This loses the version distinction needed to interpret the requested comparison.
Version-specific records make the comparison interpretable even when the underlying model is unchanged.

aipc01-0865.takeaway: Use the service-generated RAG session identifier and bind its application mapping to the correct user.
options: This gives up the conversation state the application is required to preserve.
RetrieveAndGenerate generates the first identifier; an application-generated initial ID is not the supported contract.
A user-scoped server mapping prevents accidental reuse of another conversation identifier.
The API requires the returned identifier for subsequent conversational requests.
Different users and conversations would still share state even if the tenant matches.

aipc01-0866.takeaway: Streamed tool arguments are incremental data, not independently executable operations.
options: An early parseable fragment is not proof that the tool content block is complete.
Assembly at the tool-content-block boundary preserves the complete request and avoids per-fragment execution.
Multiple tool/text blocks require separate correlation; a global concatenation can merge unrelated payloads.
Partial JSON is expected, so this turns normal streaming into avoidable retries without fixing assembly.

aipc01-0867.takeaway: Enforcement requires both the approved guardrail/version condition and coverage that cannot be bypassed by another allow.
options: An applicable explicit deny prevents a separate broad allow from authorizing missing or different guardrail use.
Permission to call a guardrail does not require every inference call to include it.
Converse and streaming authorization use the underlying inference IAM actions, so leaving the streaming action open leaves a bypass.
The condition supports the guardrail ARN with a version suffix, distinguishing version 7 from other versions.
An additional conditional allow does not cancel the already effective unconditional allow.

aipc01-0868.takeaway: A failed assessment supplies no evidence that content passed the required check.
options: Deferred checking violates the stated pre-display requirement regardless of model confidence.
Changing the content source neither fixes the dependency failure nor provides a completed output assessment.
An earlier decision on different content does not assess the new draft.
This prevents infrastructure failure from being mistaken for a successful policy result.
The bounded attempt respects the allowed wait; the fixed fallback avoids displaying an unassessed generated draft.

aipc01-0869.takeaway: Grounding validation needs an independent reference source rather than the candidate answer itself.
options: A paraphrase can preserve the same unsupported claims and does not provide an independent source.
Including the draft can make invented statements appear in their own supposed supporting reference.
A question is not the independent factual source needed to support the answer.
The source, query, and candidate response serve distinct roles in grounding and relevance checks.
A stricter threshold cannot restore independence of a reference that contains the candidate's own unsupported claims.

aipc01-0870.takeaway: Retrieved content may inform an answer but must not grant authority for side effects.
options: Helpful prompt guidance is not an enforceable boundary when the test already shows adversarial document influence.
Trusted business checks contain the impact of a model following injected instructions.
A parameter-bound confirmation prevents an informational question from silently becoming a refund action; backend policy checks still apply.
Syntactic validity does not establish permission or user intent.
Document occurrence is not verified user permission or an intentional refund request.

aipc01-0871.takeaway: Output masking and diagnostic trace sanitization are separate responsibilities.
options: The trace may carry original model output and detected values even when the displayed output is masked.
Changing the production control is unnecessary when assessment actions already provide the required distinction.
The stop reason alone does not distinguish these outcomes; assessment actions provide that detail.
This discards useful masked responses and does not distinguish the outcomes requested by operators.
The diagnostic stream remains a separate exposure of original sensitive values.

aipc01-0872.takeaway: Cached generated content must satisfy current access and evidence-validity rules before it is served.
options: Similarity does not establish current entitlement; this retains the bypass before live retrieval.
Users in one tenant can have different project entitlements, and revocation remains unhandled.
Evidence revisions can invalidate an answer even when its question and user scope appear unchanged.
This limits duration but still permits the demonstrated unauthorized response during the TTL.
The cache hit precedes retrieval, so its own validity decision must account for current permissions.

aipc01-0873.takeaway: Capacity planning must follow the embedding API's quota dimension rather than the generation model's token dashboard.
options: More unsmoothed callers can intensify the downstream request-rate bottleneck.
This targets a different model and quota from the throttled calls.
Chunk size changes request count and retrieval granularity, so the operational alternative needs a quality comparison.
Smaller vectors do not reduce the number of embedding requests made each minute.
The documented Titan embedding quota is request-based, matching the observed fourfold request increase.

aipc01-0874.takeaway: Cache economics depend on observed reuse within the cache lifetime and distinct write/read prices.
options: This ignores the higher stated cache-write charge.
With expiration before each request, $0.0125 exceeds the $0.010 uncached prefix charge and there are no observed reads to offset it.
The calculation covers only the prefix; unchanged costs must remain in the total comparison.
The stated 20-minute idle gap exceeds the specified cache lifetime.
One write plus five reads is $0.0125 + 5 × $0.001; compare it with 6 × $0.010 for the same prefix.

aipc01-0875.takeaway: Use the tested candidate reduction as a bounded optimization, then verify whole-path effects.
options: This retains the demonstrated quality gate and checks actual cost and user-facing outcomes.
The stated release gates and measured cost objective still need bounded whole-path verification.
The reported experiment compared candidate breadth with reranking enabled, not a raw-retrieval alternative.
This changes generation cost and context composition beyond the configuration actually evaluated.

aipc01-0876.takeaway: Accurate selected citations do not establish adequate support across the answer.
options: This can raise apparent citation frequency while lowering precision; claim-level correctness still matters.
The metrics expose a real tradeoff; claim-level review tests whether the prompt can preserve both requirements.
This changes the evidence requirement rather than meeting support for all material claims.
The unchanged answer length and large coverage drop show why omitting the metric hides a material regression.

aipc01-0877.takeaway: An improved average does not resolve a critical-slice regression or identify its cause.
options: Those cases become tuning data; a retained independent evaluation is needed for the final claim.
The release gate should protect the affected policy workflow and rollback to a coherent configuration.
This ignores the observed critical-slice regression and removes the stated rollback asset too soon.
Controlled replay makes the separate retrieval and generation changes interpretable.
This creates a query/index embedding mismatch rather than a coherent rollback.

aipc01-0878.takeaway: Use ingestion provenance and a coherent-space retrieval replay to isolate model-version contamination.
options: A mismatch tied to updated documents is direct evidence to investigate in the affected indexing path.
The generator can pass with supplied evidence while live retrieval remains broken.
Broader retrieval can mask some symptoms, but equal shape does not prove compatibility or test the provenance hypothesis.
A controlled re-embedding experiment tests the hypothesis without rewriting the live corpus first.
A scalar threshold does not establish alignment of model coordinate spaces, and unchanged documents miss the affected slice.
